title: AI Agent Setup
content:
Set up Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, Windsurf, Cline, Goose, or another coding agent to drive mobile, TV, desktop, and web apps with agent-device, through skills, project rules, or MCP.

In short: install the CLI, let the agent start with the requested app, and have it read the installed CLI help only for specialized work or when a command is unclear. MCP tools use the same daemon client as the CLI.

Install the CLI

npm install -g agent-device@latest

Use a global or project-local install so every agent command runs the same version. For Node, Xcode, Android SDK, macOS, and iOS device prerequisites, and for when one-off npx use is safe, see Installation.

Install the skills

If your agent client supports skills, install them after the CLI:

npx skills add callstack/agent-device

Skills come from the GitHub repository, not the npm package. The agent-device skill is the main entry point. For simulator-only work, use the iOS Simulator skill or Android Emulator skill. Skills tell the agent to start work directly and to read the installed CLI help only when the task is specialized or a command is unclear. Because the help ships with the CLI, it always matches your installed version.

Recommended agent rule

Add this rule to your agent client's project rules or custom instructions. Set up your client shows where the file goes for each client.

Use agent-device only for app/device automation tasks.
For a normal app-driving task, start immediately. Do not probe first with `--help`, `--version`, `devices`, `appstate`, `snapshot`, or `screenshot`; open the requested app in the foreground and continue from its initial interactive snapshot.
For TV, Fire TV, or Vega OS tasks, read `agent-device help tv`.
For exploratory QA, read `agent-device help dogfood`.
For logs, network, audio, traces, or runtime failures, read `agent-device help debugging`.
For React Native component internals (tree, props, state, hooks) and performance profiling (slow renders, rerenders, and their causes), read `agent-device help react-devtools`.
For React Native JavaScript heap growth, heap snapshots, allocation hotspots, or retained-object leaks, read `agent-device help cdp`.
For React Native apps, overlays, Metro/Fast Refresh blockers, and routing to profiling or debugging evidence, read `agent-device help react-native`.

Use MCP tools or the CLI in the integrated terminal.
If `agent-device` is not on PATH but the user installed it globally in another shell, resolve the command the same way the user would from a normal terminal session and run that absolute path instead. This may require inspecting shell startup behavior or package-manager/global bin locations; do not assume the agent process `PATH` is the user's `PATH`.
Do not silently fall back to `npx -y agent-device@latest`; ask or use an exact version.
MCP exposes structured tools backed by the agent-device client; it does not expose generic shell execution.
Prefer `open -> snapshot -i -> act -> re-snapshot -> verify -> close` where the target supports capture and selectors; otherwise follow target-specific help.
Use current refs such as `@e3` for exploration and selectors for durable replay.
Keep mutating commands against one session serial.
Capture screenshots, logs, network, audio, perf, traces, recordings, and `.ad` replay scripts only when they add evidence.

MCP server

agent-device mcp starts the stdio MCP server. It exposes installed CLI commands as structured tools. Some local workflows are CLI-only and have no MCP tool.

For web automation, MCP tools can target platform: "web" once the managed browser backend is set up, but agent-device web setup and agent-device web doctor are CLI-only. Run setup from a terminal that uses the same state directory as the MCP server before you ask an MCP client to drive a browser session.

MCP-only clients don't need a separately installed skill. When a client connects (initialize and server/discover), the server returns short instructions with the core workflow: start with open, act with settle: true, verify, close, how to keep refs accurate, and how to recover when the accessibility tree is sparse. An MCP-only help tool returns the same guides as agent-device help <topic|command>. Agents don't call help at startup; they call it for specialized work (gestures, scripting, TV, macOS, web, remote, debugging) or when a command is unclear.

When a tool fails, the server returns an MCP tool result with isError: true. Check the tool result, not only whether the JSON-RPC call succeeded.

The server does not run arbitrary shell commands. If the CLI is missing, the agent should ask you before installing or updating packages, reconnect the server after setup, and retry the original app-driving command without adding version or help probes.

Configuration for a global install:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "agent-device": {
      "command": "agent-device",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Without a global install, pin a version you've reviewed for unattended agent use:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "agent-device": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "agent-device@<reviewed-version>", "mcp"]
    }
  }
}

In MCP registries, the server is listed as io.github.callstack/agent-device (npm package agent-device, stdio transport). Glama lists it at callstack/agent-device.

Fix a missing agent-device command

Some agent clients run commands with a different PATH than your normal shell, so a global install that works in your terminal can be missing in the agent's terminal or MCP server. Run command -v agent-device in your own terminal and give the agent that absolute path, or use it as the MCP server command. If the path is under a version manager or a package-manager global bin directory, check your shell startup files for how that directory gets on PATH; the agent client may not load them.

Set up your agent client

Each client reads the recommended agent rule from its own location:

Client	Where the rule goes	Client-specific wrapper
Cursor	.cursor/rules/agent-device.mdc	Required .mdc frontmatter above the rule
Codex	AGENTS.md in the project root	None
Claude Code	CLAUDE.md in the project root	None; an # agent-device heading keeps it separate from other instructions
Windsurf, Cline, Goose, and others	The client's project rules or custom instructions	Whatever the client requires for a rules file

The sections below cover each client, including MCP setup.

Cursor

Cursor can use the CLI or MCP tools. Use the CLI when you want every command visible in the terminal. Add MCP when you want Cursor Agent to discover agent-device tools directly from chat.

Cursor: use the CLI

Create the rule file with the frontmatter Cursor requires:

mkdir -p .cursor/rules
cat > .cursor/rules/agent-device.mdc <<'EOF'
---
description: Use agent-device for app and device automation
alwaysApply: true
---

REPLACE THIS LINE with the recommended agent rule from https://oss.callstack.com/agent-device/docs/agent-setup#recommended-agent-rule
EOF

Open .cursor/rules/agent-device.mdc and replace the placeholder line with the recommended agent rule. Then ask Cursor Agent to run:

agent-device open <app-or-url> --platform ios --foreground

Cursor: use MCP tools

Create a project MCP config:

mkdir -p .cursor
cat > .cursor/mcp.json <<'JSON'
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "agent-device": {
      "command": "agent-device",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}
JSON

Restart Cursor or reconnect MCP in Cursor settings, then ask Cursor Agent:

Use the agent-device MCP tools to inspect the iOS app. Open the app, take an interactive snapshot, act on visible refs/selectors, verify with another snapshot, and close the session.

If the MCP server fails to start because Cursor can't find the global binary, use the absolute binary path in .cursor/mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "agent-device": {
      "command": "/absolute/path/to/agent-device",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Codex

Paste the recommended agent rule into AGENTS.md in the project root, or into the project instructions, then let Codex run agent-device in the terminal:

agent-device open <app-or-url> --platform ios --foreground

If Codex can't find agent-device, see Fix a missing agent-device command.

For reviews or planning-only tasks, tell the agent not to touch devices unless you ask.

Claude Code

Claude Code can use agent-device from the terminal or from the VS Code extension. The VS Code extension uses MCP servers you add with the claude CLI and manage with /mcp.

Claude Code: use the CLI

Open CLAUDE.md in the project root, creating it if it doesn't exist. Add an # agent-device heading and paste the recommended agent rule below it. Keep any instructions already in the file.

Then ask Claude Code to run:

agent-device open <app-or-url> --platform android --foreground

Claude Code: use MCP tools

Add a user-scoped server:

claude mcp add --transport stdio --scope user agent-device -- agent-device mcp
claude mcp list

Or add it to the current project so teammates can review the generated .mcp.json:

claude mcp add --transport stdio --scope project agent-device -- agent-device mcp

In Claude Code or the VS Code extension, run:

/mcp

Confirm agent-device is connected, then ask:

Use the agent-device MCP tools to verify the app. Open the app, take an interactive snapshot, use refs/selectors for actions, verify with another snapshot, and close the session.

If Claude Code can't start the MCP server because the extension can't find the global binary, remove the server and add it again with an absolute path:

claude mcp remove agent-device
claude mcp add --transport stdio --scope user agent-device -- /absolute/path/to/agent-device mcp

You can still run CLI commands in the integrated terminal for long-running or manual workflows.

Windsurf, Cline, Goose, and other MCP clients

If the client supports mcpServers, use the MCP server configuration, then tell the agent to use MCP tools or terminal CLI commands for device work.

If the client supports project rules or custom instructions, paste the recommended agent rule there, inside any wrapper the client requires for a rules file. If it doesn't, ask the agent to open the requested app and continue from the initial interactive snapshot; point it to a help topic only when the task is specialized or a command is unclear.

Related pages

For supported targets, evidence features, and how agent-device differs from scripted test frameworks, see Introduction. For command groups and platform behavior, see Commands.

For the local execution model, permissions, artifacts, and sensitive data guidance, see Security & Trust.

Agent-readable docs

Use llms-full.txt when an agent needs the whole documentation as one text file. For exact command syntax, the installed CLI help is authoritative:

agent-device help
agent-device help workflow
agent-device help dogfood

title: AI SDK
description: Use agent-device/ai-sdk to give an AI SDK agent a typed set of tools for navigating and inspecting an app. The tools run in-process, share one named session, and by default cover the core loop of reading the screen and acting on it. Make an iOS simulator or device available to agent-device, then configure an AI SDK model. String model IDs use AI Gateway by default: Alternatively, pass a model from your configured AI SDK provider. See the AI SDK guide to choosing a provider. Set AI_MODEL to a model available through your configured AI SDK provider. The agent decides which device tools to call to complete the prompt. The returned client targets the same session; close it in finally so the device is released even if generation fails.

title: AWS Device Farm
content:
Use AWS Device Farm to run agent-device on hosted Android and iOS devices through remote-access WebDriver sessions. You need an AWS account with a Device Farm project and the AWS CLI installed. AWS Device Farm does not cover Vega OS: agent-device rejects a Vega Fire TV ARN. For Vega, use a local Vega Virtual Device (VVD).

Set credentials and connect

agent-device runs aws devicefarm ..., so it uses the AWS CLI credential provider chain and works with any non-interactive AWS CLI credential source in CI. You do not need aws login. See the AWS CLI environment variable reference for supported credential sources.

Use short-lived CI credentials instead of long-lived IAM user keys. In GitHub Actions, use OIDC to assume an IAM role and let the action export the standard AWS environment variables. AWS documents IAM OIDC providers, and the official configure-aws-credentials action documents the GitHub Actions setup.

For example, a CI job can set:

export AWS_REGION=us-west-2
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=... # present for temporary credentials

AWS web identity flows can use:

export AWS_ROLE_ARN=arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/<role-name>
export AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE=/path/to/token
export AWS_REGION=us-west-2

Connect with the Device Farm project, the device, and an optional app upload:

agent-device connect aws-device-farm \
  --platform android \
  --aws-project-arn arn:aws:devicefarm:us-west-2:<account-id>:project:<project-id> \
  --aws-device-arn arn:aws:devicefarm:us-west-2::device:<device-id> \
  --aws-app-arn arn:aws:devicefarm:us-west-2:<account-id>:upload:<upload-id>

Omit --aws-app-arn when the remote-access session does not need an uploaded app. You can also pass the ARNs through environment variables:

export AWS_DEVICE_FARM_PROJECT_ARN=...
export AWS_DEVICE_FARM_DEVICE_ARN=...
export AWS_DEVICE_FARM_APP_ARN=...

agent-device also accepts AGENT_DEVICE_AWS_DEVICE_FARM_PROJECT_ARN, AGENT_DEVICE_AWS_DEVICE_FARM_DEVICE_ARN, and AGENT_DEVICE_AWS_DEVICE_FARM_APP_ARN as aliases.

connect makes read-only get-project, get-device, and, when you pass an app, get-upload calls. It rejects a device or app for the wrong platform, and an app upload that is not ready. You cannot install an app once the remote-access session is allocated. When an app is required, run the printed reconnect command, including --session <name> --force, before open.

Run a session from the CLI

Every connect without --session creates a new connection, and the printed next steps include its generated --session. Keep that flag on every command when several processes or CI jobs share a host; the active connection is safe only for one sequential workflow. To replace a named connection, run connect ... --session <name> --force. --force without --session creates a new connection and leaves existing sessions untouched.

export AWS_REGION=us-west-2
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=...

agent-device connect aws-device-farm \
  --platform android \
  --aws-project-arn "$AWS_DEVICE_FARM_PROJECT_ARN" \
  --aws-device-arn "$AWS_DEVICE_FARM_DEVICE_ARN" \
  --aws-app-arn "$AWS_DEVICE_FARM_APP_ARN" \
  --provider-session-name "$GITHUB_JOB"

agent-device open com.example.app
agent-device snapshot -i
agent-device close
agent-device artifacts --json
agent-device disconnect

To drive AWS Device Farm only through MCP, see Use a provider only through MCP.

Use the Node.js client

Configure the client directly when your Node.js process manages the AWS credentials and selectors:

const client = createAgentDeviceClient({
  leaseProvider: 'aws-device-farm',
  platform: 'android',
  awsProjectArn: process.env.AWS_DEVICE_FARM_PROJECT_ARN,
  awsDeviceArn: process.env.AWS_DEVICE_FARM_DEVICE_ARN,
  awsAppArn: process.env.AWS_DEVICE_FARM_APP_ARN,
  awsRegion: process.env.AWS_REGION,
});

await client.apps.open({ app: 'com.example.app' });
const closed = await client.sessions.close();

Get artifacts and troubleshoot

After close, AWS Device Farm can return remote-access video and log artifacts once it finalizes them. The provider session ID is the remote-access session ARN. See Retrieve artifacts after close.

If connect fails, use the reported aws devicefarm get-* error to check the credential chain, ARN, region, resource platform, or upload readiness. A failed connect has not allocated a device yet.

To enter text, see Fill text on hosted WebDriver sessions.

On a screen that never goes still, such as a looping video, a live ticker, or continuous animation, snapshot -i can time out while screenshot of the same screen still returns. On a metered device every second of that read is billed, so do not retry the snapshot in a loop. Take a screenshot instead and drive from @refs an earlier snapshot captured. --depth trims the tree after it arrives, so it cannot shorten a read that never finishes. See Snapshots for details.

title: Batching
content:
Use batch to run several commands in one daemon request. It saves round trips when you already know
the next sequence of actions.

The whole batch has a 60-second wall-clock budget within a 90-second client timeout. At the
budget, the running step receives the same cancellation as a canceled request. When that step
settles, a failed batch returns COMMAND_FAILED with details.reason: daemon_request_timeout.
The daemon and other sessions stay available if it responds to the client. A close step may
already have ended its session. A failed batch keeps
details.executed, details.partialResults, and its dispatch status, so you can continue from
the failing step. A batch that completes every step returns success even if it settles shortly
after the deadline. Cancellation does not prove that native device work has stopped. If a step
ignores cancellation beyond the remaining 30 seconds, the client may report a transport timeout.
For a daemon that does not respond, the client's existing liveness check can reset it. Split
longer sequences into separate requests.

Some resource operations cannot run as bounded steps. The failed step returns
details.reason: bounded_composite_resource_unsupported, details.shape,
details.dispatched: no, and details.standaloneCommandName for a known public command. The name
is not a complete command. Affected commands include perf, audio, record, trace, and some
logs operations. A close that would dispose an owned resource or release a provider lease, and
acquisition that would recover another session's durable resources, can also be refused. Opening
another app in the same session keeps its owned resource handles. An Android test IME alone is
restored by ordinary close, including a bounded step. Restoration may settle after the remaining
batch time. If it fails, the session retires and the device claim stays for recovery; inspect the
device and claim before acting. Run a refused step separately with its original arguments and options, the same --session value, and
the same private CLI context. Inspect details.partialResults and
details.dispatchedSteps before retrying the batch: earlier steps may already have changed the app.
The batch still authenticates and renews its own lease while it runs.

Run a batch from the CLI

From a file:

agent-device batch \
  --session sim \
  --platform ios \
  --udid 00008150-001849640CF8401C \
  --steps-file /tmp/batch-steps.json \
  --json

Inline, for small payloads:

agent-device batch --steps '[{"command":"open","input":{"app":"settings"}},{"command":"wait","input":{"kind":"duration","durationMs":100}}]'

Step payload format

Pass batch a JSON array of steps:

[
  { "command": "open", "input": { "app": "settings" } },
  {
    "command": "wait",
    "input": { "kind": "selector", "selector": "label=\"Privacy & Security\"", "timeoutMs": 3000 }
  },
  {
    "command": "click",
    "input": { "target": { "kind": "selector", "selector": "label=\"Privacy & Security\"" } }
  },
  {
    "command": "get",
    "input": { "format": "text", "target": { "kind": "selector", "selector": "label=\"Tracking\"" } }
  }
]

Notes:

input is required and takes the same fields as the matching MCP or Node client command.

A step can only have command, input, and runtime keys; any other key is rejected.

Steps written as positionals/flags are rejected. Rewrite each step with structured input, for example {"command":"open","input":{"app":"settings","platform":"ios"}}.

batch and replay steps can't be nested inside a batch.

--on-error stop is the only error mode: the batch stops at the first failing step.

A batch runs at most 100 steps by default. Pass --max-steps <n> to raise or lower the limit, up to 1000.

A step without platform uses the batch's --platform. Session lock defaults don't override it.

Steps use the same session binding and session lock mode as the batch command itself.

Response shape

Success:

{
  "success": true,
  "data": {
    "total": 4,
    "executed": 4,
    "totalDurationMs": 1810,
    "results": [
      { "step": 1, "command": "open", "ok": true, "durationMs": 1020 },
      { "step": 2, "command": "wait", "ok": true, "durationMs": 320 },
      { "step": 3, "command": "click", "ok": true, "durationMs": 260 },
      { "step": 4, "command": "get", "ok": true, "durationMs": 210, "data": { "text": "..." } }
    ]
  }
}

Without --json, batch prints the overall completion line followed by a short summary of each step.

Failure:

{
  "success": false,
  "error": {
    "code": "COMMAND_FAILED",
    "message": "Batch failed at step 3 (click): ...",
    "details": {
      "step": 3,
      "command": "click",
      "executed": 2,
      "total": 4,
      "partialResults": [
        { "step": 1, "command": "open", "ok": true },
        { "step": 2, "command": "wait", "ok": true }
      ]
    }
  }
}

Tips for agents

Keep each batch to one screen flow.

After steps that change the UI (open, click, fill, swipe), add a wait or is exists step before reads that matter.

Treat earlier refs and snapshots as stale after the UI changes.

Prefer --steps-file over inline JSON.

Keep batches to about 5-20 steps.

When a batch fails, inspect details.step, details.partialResults, and details.dispatchedSteps before retrying.

Example recipes

Open app -> open thread -> type -> send

[
  { "command": "open", "input": { "app": "com.example.chat", "platform": "android" } },
  { "command": "wait", "input": { "kind": "text", "text": "Inbox", "timeoutMs": 3000 } },
  { "command": "press", "input": { "target": { "kind": "selector", "selector": "label=\"Inbox\" role=button" } } },
  { "command": "press", "input": { "target": { "kind": "selector", "selector": "label=\"Morgan Lee\"" } } },
  {
    "command": "fill",
    "input": {
      "target": { "kind": "selector", "selector": "label=\"Message\" role=text-field" },
      "text": "sent the update"
    }
  },
  { "command": "press", "input": { "target": { "kind": "selector", "selector": "label=\"Send\" role=button" } } },
  { "command": "wait", "input": { "kind": "text", "text": "sent the update", "timeoutMs": 3000 } }
]

Open app -> open action menu -> choose option -> verify

[
  { "command": "open", "input": { "app": "com.example.app", "platform": "android" } },
  { "command": "wait", "input": { "kind": "text", "text": "Home", "timeoutMs": 3000 } },
  {
    "command": "press",
    "input": { "target": { "kind": "selector", "selector": "label=\"More actions\" role=button" } }
  },
  { "command": "wait", "input": { "kind": "text", "text": "Scan document", "timeoutMs": 2000 } },
  { "command": "press", "input": { "target": { "kind": "selector", "selector": "label=\"Scan document\"" } } },
  { "command": "wait", "input": { "kind": "text", "text": "Document uploaded", "timeoutMs": 15000 } },
  { "command": "is", "input": { "predicate": "visible", "selector": "label=\"Document uploaded\"" } }
]

Avoid acting on a stale accessibility tree

The accessibility tree can lag behind fast UI changes. Add explicit waits, and split long workflows
into separate batches by phase:

navigate

verify/extract

cleanup

title: BrowserStack
content:
Use BrowserStack App Automate to run agent-device on hosted Android and iOS devices over WebDriver. You need a BrowserStack account with App Automate access.

Set credentials and connect

Export your BrowserStack credentials, for example from CI secrets:

export BROWSERSTACK_USERNAME=...
export BROWSERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY=...

Connect with the platform, exact device and OS version, and app to test:

agent-device connect browserstack \
  --platform android \
  --device "Google Pixel 8" \
  --provider-os-version 14.0 \
  --provider-app bs://app-id

--provider-app accepts a BrowserStack app reference such as bs://..., an HTTP(S) app URL, or an existing local app path. agent-device uploads a local path when it creates the hosted session.

connect verifies the BrowserStack credentials and the exact device/OS pair. It checks a bs:// reference against recent uploads, and confirms that a local app file exists before saving its absolute path. A public URL is saved as-is; BrowserStack validates it when the session starts. open takes the app's installed package or bundle identifier, not its upload name.

If you change credentials while the daemon runs, see Change credentials while the daemon runs.

Optional labels:

--provider-project agent-device
--provider-build "$GITHUB_RUN_ID"
--provider-session-name "$GITHUB_JOB"

Optional device features:

--provider-device-orientation portrait   # or landscape        (alias --device-orientation)
--provider-geo-location US                                   # (alias --geo-location)
--provider-timezone New_York                                 # (alias --timezone)
--provider-appium-version 3.2.0                              # (alias --appium-version)
--provider-language Fr                                       # (alias --language)
--provider-locale Fr                                         # (alias --locale)
--provider-network-profile 4g-lte-advanced-good              # (alias --network-profile)
--provider-custom-network 1000                               # (alias --custom-network)
--provider-no-resign-app                                     # iOS only

agent-device sends these values to BrowserStack as bstack:options capabilities when it creates the hosted session.

The orientation applies when the session starts. An activity without a fixed orientation, such as a Chrome Custom Tab hosting OAuth, can still open in landscape. Run agent-device orientation portrait after it opens if you need portrait.

--provider-appium-version pins the Appium server BrowserStack runs for the session. Without it, BrowserStack runs its default Appium 1.x, and mobile: commands such as deepLink and pressButton need Appium 2.x or newer.

--provider-network-profile and --provider-custom-network are mutually exclusive.

--provider-no-resign-app applies to iOS only. BrowserStack re-signs uploaded iOS apps with its provisioning profile, which strips entitlements. Pass this flag when you test features that need entitlements, such as push notifications.

Run a session from the CLI

export BROWSERSTACK_USERNAME=...
export BROWSERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY=...

agent-device connect browserstack \
  --platform android \
  --device "Google Pixel 8" \
  --provider-os-version 14.0 \
  --provider-app bs://app-id \
  --provider-project agent-device \
  --provider-build "$GITHUB_RUN_ID"

agent-device open com.example.app
agent-device snapshot -i
agent-device click 'label="Continue"'
agent-device close
agent-device artifacts --json
agent-device disconnect

To drive BrowserStack only through MCP, see Use a provider only through MCP.

Use the Node.js client

Configure the client directly when your Node.js process manages the BrowserStack credentials and selectors instead of a saved CLI connection profile:

const client = createAgentDeviceClient({
  leaseProvider: 'browserstack',
  platform: 'android',
  device: 'Google Pixel 8',
  providerOsVersion: '14.0',
  providerApp: 'bs://app-id',
  providerProject: 'agent-device',
  providerBuild: process.env.GITHUB_RUN_ID,
});

await client.apps.open({ app: 'com.example.app' });
const snapshot = await client.capture.snapshot({ interactiveOnly: true });
console.log(snapshot.nodes.slice(0, 5));
await client.interactions.click({ selector: 'label="Continue"' });
const closed = await client.sessions.close();
const providerSessionId = closed.provider?.providerSessionId;

if (providerSessionId) {
  const artifacts = await client.sessions.artifacts({
    provider: 'browserstack',
    providerSessionId,
  });
  console.log(artifacts.cloudArtifacts);
}

Get artifacts and troubleshoot

After close, BrowserStack can return session video, Appium logs, device logs, dashboard URLs, and public URLs. The provider session ID is the WebDriver session ID. See Retrieve artifacts after close.

BrowserStack errors distinguish rejected credentials, an unavailable device/OS pair, a missing bs:// upload, and a missing local app file.

To enter text, see Fill text on hosted WebDriver sessions.

title: Build an integration
content:
This page is for developers who build a bridge, remote daemon, device-cloud backend, or in-process runner on top of agent-device. These entry points let your server own device access, command dispatch, or Metro while reusing agent-device's behavior.

To drive devices from your own Node.js code, use the Node.js API instead.

Runnable examples

The repository includes runnable, typechecked examples for these entry points:

Example	Demonstrates
batch-orchestration.ts	Run a batch through a custom transport
metro-runtime.ts	Normalize a Metro URL and resolve runtime transport hints

Build the package with pnpm build, then run an example with Node:

node --experimental-strip-types examples/sdk/metro-runtime.ts

API reference

Entry points for integrations:

agent-device/android-adb
createAndroidPortReverseManager(provider) / createAndroidPortReverseManager(executor, { noRebind })

AndroidKeyboardState, AndroidKeyboardDismissResult, AndroidPortReverseEndpoint

types: RemoteConfigProfile

Android ADB providers

Use agent-device/android-adb when your bridge owns Android device access and you want
agent-device's behavior for ADB operations. Executors receive the arguments that follow adb, so a
remote bridge can route the same argument arrays through an ADB tunnel, websocket API, or another
remote transport.

The helpers take an executor directly. Use captureAndroidLogcatWithAdb(executor, options?) for a
bounded logcat capture.

A provider can also expose reverse to own port reversal. Plain executors do not advertise reverse
support; call createAndroidPortReverseManager(providerOrExecutor)
only when the provider supports adb reverse argument semantics. The manager makes duplicate setup
idempotent for the same owner and rejects conflicting owners for the same local endpoint. For a
device that other adb clients also drive, pass an executor with { noRebind: true }: the manager
runs adb reverse --no-rebind and never replaces an existing device mapping, including one it
created. When adb reverse --list shows the mapping, the refusal fails with COMMAND_FAILED and
details.reason: 'android_port_reverse_rebind_refused'. Otherwise it fails as an ordinary adb error.

The device shell re-parses whatever follows shell or exec-out, so those commands are built for you:
every dynamic word is rendered for the quoting its transport applies before it reaches the device. adb
forwards words verbatim, so a word is single-quoted; hdc wraps each element it sends in double quotes,
where $, a backquote, and " stay live, so a word is escaped for that context instead. An array that
begins with shell or exec-out and did not come from those builders is refused with INVALID_ARGS and
details.reason: 'unguarded-device-shell-argv' instead of being dispatched. A bridge that composes its
own device commands calls runAdbShell(executor, words, options?) or
runAdbExecOut(executor, words, options?) from agent-device/android-adb, passing each value as its
own word; runAndroidShell(device, words, options?) and runAndroidExecOut(device, words, options?)
resolve the executor from a device instead.

const provider = {
  exec: async (args: readonly string[], options?: AndroidAdbExecutorOptions) =>
    await runAdbThroughRemoteTunnel(args, options),
};

const apps = await listAndroidAppsWithAdb(provider.exec); // user-installed apps by default
const foreground = await getAndroidAppStateWithAdb(provider.exec);

Batch orchestration for custom transports

Use agent-device/batch when a bridge or in-process runner receives daemon-shaped requests but owns command dispatch itself. The helper applies the same validation, inherited flags, serial execution, partial results, and error envelopes as the daemon batch command.

Full example from examples/sdk/batch-orchestration.ts:

Remote Metro helpers

const remoteConfig = resolveRemoteConfigProfile({
  configPath: './agent-device.remote.json',
  cwd: process.cwd(),
});

const prepared = await prepareMetroRuntime({
  projectRoot: remoteConfig.profile.metroProjectRoot!,
  kind: remoteConfig.profile.metroKind ?? 'auto',
  proxyBaseUrl: remoteConfig.profile.metroProxyBaseUrl,
  proxyBearerToken: remoteConfig.profile.metroBearerToken,
  bridgeScope: {
    tenantId: remoteConfig.profile.tenant!,
    runId: remoteConfig.profile.runId!,
    leaseId: remoteConfig.profile.leaseId!,
  },
  companionProfileKey: remoteConfig.resolvedPath,
});

console.log(prepared.iosRuntime, prepared.androidRuntime);

await reloadMetro({
  runtime: prepared.iosRuntime,
});

await stopMetroTunnel({
  projectRoot: remoteConfig.profile.metroProjectRoot!,
  profileKey: remoteConfig.resolvedPath,
});

Use agent-device/remote-config for profile loading and path resolution, agent-device/metro for Metro preparation, reload, and tunnel lifecycle, and agent-device/contracts when a server consumer needs daemon request or runtime contract types. For bridged remote Metro, proxyBaseUrl is the bridge origin and publicBaseUrl is optional; the bridge descriptor supplies cloud iOS wildcard HTTPS hints and Android runtime-route hints. reloadMetro() calls Metro's /reload endpoint, matching the terminal r reload path for connected React Native apps.

stopMetroTunnel() releases a companion once per consumer, so it only returns once the companion is gone when it releases the last one. If that companion belongs to another user — you started it with sudo, for example — the call fails with its pid, and the profile keeps tracking it so a later stop retries the same process instead of starting a second companion beside it. Stop the surviving process as its owner (sudo kill <pid>) and run stopMetroTunnel() again.

Selector helpers

Use agent-device/selectors to parse and match selector expressions in a remote daemon or bridge. The role= term matches the platform-neutral kind vocabulary that snapshot --json publishes (see Snapshots): pass the nodes as captured, and a node whose kind is text always matches role=text. Separately, the deprecated raw leaf spellings (statictext, edittext, textview, …) also match, each on the nodes that actually carried that class. A leaf spelling matches beside such a node's kind, not in place of it — role=webarea resolves a macOS-helper AXWebArea node whose kind is axwebarea, for example. Matching stays platform-aware because editability checks differ by backend.

listSelectorChainMatches(nodes, chain, options) returns every node the winning selector alternative matches, in snapshot order, plus that alternative and its index — the same first-match domain findSelectorChainMatch uses, without uniqueness refusal, so a runner applies its own strictness to the same nodes the CLI matched. resolveSelectorChain can name a later alternative: by default it refuses an ambiguous one and keeps walking, so the indices agree when it passes requireUnique: false, when the first matching alternative is unique, or when disambiguateAmbiguous: true resolves that alternative in place. It returns null when no alternative matches. findSelectorChainMatch and listSelectorChainMatches take { platform, requireRect? }; resolveSelectorChain also takes requireUnique? (default true) and disambiguateAmbiguous?. The matched SnapshotNode objects are the ones passed in.

const chain = parseSelectorChain('role=button label="Continue" visible=true');

const match = findSelectorChainMatch(snapshot.nodes, chain, {
  platform: 'android',
  requireRect: true,
});

if (!match) {
  // Build a daemon-shaped error with formatSelectorFailure(...) if needed.
}

The target tables below are generated from the runtime command-admission facts that back the capabilities command: a command that leaves the code leaves this page. Labels, limits, and integration rows are maintained beside the generator, and command availability does not establish support for every operation, subcommand, or device model.
It covers agent-device 0.21.34-dev, generated 2026-10-27.

Yes means the facts admit every command in that row on the target and every operation the row advertises. No means at least one is refused. A qualified cell names the operations that answer there. Targets that share the same available operations print as one column.

Physical iOS devices discovered only through xctrace use the XCTest backend rather than CoreDevice: they support open/close, interactions, snapshots, and screenshots, while app inventory, installation, logs, performance sampling, recording, deep links, and launch arguments need CoreDevice.

One capability depends on the agent machine rather than the target: system audio sampling works only when the daemon runs on macOS, which is what this page assumes.

Check the device in front of you rather than trusting a table:

agent-device capabilities --platform ios --device "iPhone 17 Pro"
agent-device capabilities --session my-session --json

A provider column answers for that provider in its default configuration. Provider credentials, device selection, and artifact retrieval live on the provider pages.

Native profiles and traces	Use perf cpu profile for Apple xctrace or Android simpleperf profiles, and perf trace for supported Apple xctrace or Android Perfetto captures; both need a supported app session. The separate trace command captures session diagnostic logs.	Native profiles and traces
.ad replay scripts and the replay test runner	Runs supported .ad actions subject to target support and replay restrictions. Some resource operations are unavailable inside bounded replay even when they work standalone.	.ad replay scripts and the replay test runner
Batched command runs	Runs registry-approved batch commands serially in one session. Target admission still applies, and lifecycle and resource restrictions can reject operations that work standalone.	Batched command runs
Maestro flow import and .ad export	Runs a documented subset of Maestro YAML on iOS and Android only. Exports compatible .ad actions to Maestro YAML; unsupported actions and selector shapes fail with source context, and semantic differences produce warnings.	Maestro flow import and .ad export
MCP server	One agent-device mcp server per daemon exposes the device commands that mark themselves MCP-exposed, including provider sessions already connected on that daemon.	MCP server
Typed Node.js API	The typed client exposes device and session operations through domain methods and client.command. Daemon-backed methods share CLI command semantics and target restrictions; the client does not expose every CLI entry point.	Typed Node.js API
Named sessions, leases, and parallel runs	Sessions and leases are daemon state, so parallel runs come from separate session names, device allowlists, and worktrees rather than from the target. Two worktrees can drive two platforms from one checkout.	Named sessions, leases, and parallel runs
Remote daemon and device host	A proxy between the agent machine and the device host forwards the same daemon surface, so the device rows above apply across it. Provider clouds need no proxy.	Remote daemon and device host
Hosted device providers	BrowserStack, AWS Device Farm, TestMu AI, and Limrun appear as their own columns above. Provider artifact lookup after close works for the three WebDriver providers; Limrun keeps no artifacts.	Hosted device providers
Native, React Native, Expo, and Flutter apps	Native and Flutter apps use the interactions and accessibility data exposed by their target. React Native and Expo development builds can additionally expose React component inspection, render profiling, and Metro CDP tools when their documented prerequisites are met.	Native, React Native, Expo, and Flutter apps

title: Commands
content:
Find the command for a task, the flags it takes, and how it behaves on each platform.

For persistent defaults and project-scoped CLI settings, see Configuration.

CLI help matches your installed version. agent-device help lists the workflow and platform guides, and help <command> gives a command's exact flags:

agent-device help
agent-device help commands
agent-device help workflow
agent-device help open

If your agent runtime supports skills, install them to route agents automatically; they are optional. The CLI help topics are the reference for your installed version.

For MCP-aware clients that support direct tools, run:

agent-device mcp

For MCP client setup and what MCP does not expose, see AI Agent Setup.

Output and warnings

In text mode, every command prints each response warning as a Warning: line after its own output.
get, find, clipboard, and record print those lines on stderr instead, so
value=$(agent-device get text …) captures only the value. With --json, warnings stay in
data.warnings and no Warning: line is printed.

Navigation

agent-device boot
agent-device boot --platform ios
agent-device boot --platform android
agent-device boot --platform android --device Pixel_9_Pro_XL --headless
agent-device shutdown --platform ios
agent-device shutdown --platform android --device Pixel_9_Pro_XL
agent-device open [app|url] [url]
agent-device open --platform macos --surface frontmost-app
agent-device open --platform macos --surface desktop
agent-device close [app]
agent-device back
agent-device back --in-app
agent-device back --system
agent-device home
agent-device orientation portrait
agent-device orientation landscape-left
agent-device orientation auto
agent-device app-switcher
agent-device action-button
agent-device hardware-button volume-up
agent-device hardware-button volume-down
agent-device hardware-button power
agent-device fold closed
agent-device fold half-open
agent-device fold open
agent-device telephony call 5551234
agent-device telephony cancel 5551234
agent-device telephony sms 5551234 "Your code is 1234"
agent-device device status --platform android --serial emulator-5554
agent-device device release --stale
agent-device daemon stop --clean
agent-device daemon status --json

Boot and shut down:

boot gets the selected target ready without launching an app. It needs an active session or a device selector. You mainly need it when open fails because no simulator or emulator is booted.

Android: boot --platform android --device <avd-name> launches that emulator with a window; add --headless to launch it without one. On macOS the window opens behind the focused app, which keeps focus (also when open boots a stopped AVD). This is best-effort: the emulator can still take focus if the focused app cannot be read, or if its window appears after the startup budget runs out.

shutdown turns off the selected Apple simulator or Android emulator. It refuses the active session's device; use close --shutdown to end the session and turn the device off.

--timeout <ms> on boot, open <app>, and prepare ios-runner is the startup budget for booting an iOS Simulator or Android emulator (for prepare ios-runner, shared with runner preparation). A never-booted iOS Simulator can take several minutes. When the budget runs out, the command fails with error.details.reason: boot_timeout and the device keeps booting, so a retry finds it further along. See Sessions.

Select a device:

--platform apple is an alias for the Apple backend (ios, tvOS, macOS). Add --target mobile|tv|desktop to --platform to choose phone/tablet, TV, or desktop targets.

A command that needs one device fails with AMBIGUOUS_MATCH and lists the candidates when you pass no --device, --udid, or --serial and several are equally preferred, such as two booted emulators. Virtual devices are preferred over physical ones and booted over offline ones first, and commands inside a session use the session's device. devices still lists everything.

Commands without --session use an implicit session scoped to your worktree and the selected platform. For named sessions, AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION, and --session-lock reject|strip, see Sessions.

Device claims and the daemon:

device status lists host-local device claims without starting or contacting a daemon; --stale shows the stale claims it hides by default (owner exited, PID reused, state directory deleted, or daemon replaced), some of whose owners may still be running. Scope it with --platform plus --udid (Apple) or --serial (Android). A claim held by another live or uncertain owner blocks open, unless the device rebooted after the claim was taken: then open settles that owner's durable resources, takes the claim, and reports the release in warnings.

device release --stale settles the durable resources of an owner that provably can't release its claim (its process exited or a newer daemon replaced it), then clears the claim. Live, uncertain, PID-reused, corrupt, and deleted-state-directory claims are refused with the reason. See Sessions.

A command that needs the shared local daemon starts it for its state directory when none runs; device status and device release --stale never contact one. When the running daemon comes from another version or build, the command replaces it only if it reports no work: no request in flight, no session, no repair session and no live lease. A resumable upload still streaming and a host human-control hold that names no lease are not counted, so a replacement can end them. Otherwise the command fails with daemon-busy and leaves the daemon alone. A daemon from a release that predates this check is never replaced, and fails with daemon-incompatible. End a busy or older daemon deliberately with daemon stop. Node.js clients choose this per client; see Daemon lifecycle.

daemon stop --state-dir <path> stops a detached local daemon with process signals after verifying its identity. --clean also removes the Apple runner processes and leases that daemon retained.

daemon stop refuses a live embedded runtime with details.reason: daemon-owner-embedded and a hint naming the host PID. Close it in its host process with the handle returned by startAgentDevice(). Stop refuses live unrecognized ownership with daemon-owner-unrecognized. Neither refusal sends a request or signal. Stop retires an embedded or unrecognized registration when its recorded host lifetime has provably exited. Without --clean, an unreadable daemon.json fails with daemon-record-unreadable. --clean requires proven detached ownership; embedded, unrecognized and unreadable records fail with daemon-clean-not-detached. daemon status shows host-owned or owner-not-recognized. See Daemon lifecycle.

daemon status [--state-dir <path>] [--json] reads the daemon's record without contacting it. For a running daemon it lists every provider it registered, built in or installed, and the reason any plugin failed to register. See provider plugins.

Open apps and links:

open [app|url] [url] boots the selected device when needed and opens the target in a session. open <url> opens deep links on Android and iOS, and open <app> <url> opens a deep link in that app on iOS. See Desktop targets for macOS activation behavior.

On iOS devices, http(s):// URLs open in Safari when no app is active. Custom-scheme URLs need an active app in the session.

open <app> --wait <ms> waits up to that budget for a device another session holds, then fails with DEVICE_IN_USE. The wait extends the command's timeout, so you don't need a longer --timeout. A claim held by another workspace's daemon is not waited for; open returns its recovery command at once. Device-mutating commands like install and reinstall never wait either: a claim held by another session fails them at once, and when the caller sends a workspace, another workspace's claim under the same session name fails too. See Sessions.

open <app> --launch-console <path> captures launch-time stdout/stderr for local iOS simulator app launches. It is not valid for URL opens or other targets.

open --platform macos --surface app|frontmost-app|desktop|menubar selects the macOS session surface; app is the default when you name an app. See Desktop targets. --save-script records the surface so replay reopens it; with no surface given, replay opens an app session.

Android React Native: open --relaunch needs an installed package name. Install or reinstall the APK first; open <apk|aab> --relaunch is rejected. For Metro-backed JS changes, run metro reload before reaching for open <app> --relaunch.

Android (adb): an intent target such as open settings records the package that opened as appBundleId. open settings --relaunch stops and restarts that app. If the intent matches more than one activity, --relaunch fails.

Android (ADB): close force-stops the app, then checks for 2 seconds that it has left the foreground and for 2 more that its process has exited. If either check window ends first, close fails with details.reason: android-app-close-timeout and details.phase set to foreground or process; apps Android restarts at once, such as the launcher, fail this way.

iOS Simulator launch behavior:

An open that launches an app reports timing.postOpenObservation. When it is present and not "observable", the next command that reads the screen waits briefly until two reads agree, so a click lands where the element comes to rest. If the screen is still moving after that wait, the command proceeds and warns that the surface was still changing.

If CoreSimulator never answers a URL hand-off, open fails within 20 seconds with details.reason: ios-simulator-openurl-timeout. The Simulator may still have received the URL; retry the open or answer the prompt with alert accept.

When open <app> --launch-url <url> raises an Open in "<App>"? prompt and the URL's scheme belongs to the session app, open taps Open and returns launchConfirmation: "accepted". If the app still never starts, open hands over the URL once more.

When that prompt stays unanswered, open returns launchConfirmation: "unanswered" with launchConfirmationReason: alert-unrecognized for a prompt it did not recognize (such as a non-English Simulator), or url-owner-unresolved when no single installed app owns the URL's scheme or that lookup failed. The prompt stays on screen; warnings name the next step. For url-owner-unresolved, answer the prompt with alert accept. For alert-unrecognized, read the alert with alert get first: it can be the app's own alert, such as a permission prompt, rather than a translated launch confirmation. Answer with alert accept only when it is the launch confirmation.

When open could not read whether a prompt is up at all (the alert read, the accept, or the runner itself failed), open succeeds with launchConfirmationProbeFailure set to alert-read, alert-accept, or runner and no launchConfirmation, plus a warning to check with alert get before retrying.

details.reason: launch_confirmation_unanswered means the app never started after the prompt was accepted, or the prompt stayed visible after a failed tap. Answer it with alert accept or alert dismiss before continuing.

details.reason: launch_confirmation_foreign_app means another installed app owns the scheme (details.foreignAppBundleId). Close the prompt with alert dismiss and pass a URL your app handles.

A prompt that appears after open has already seen the app is not reported and not answered; use alert accept.

Back, orientation, and hardware buttons:

back uses app-owned back navigation: visible in-app back UI on Apple targets, and the back keyevent on Android. --in-app names this default explicitly.

On iOS, a single-screen iPhone or an iPad whose app provably fills its screen, back can use a top-leading tap when the app tree is unreadable. It compares the screen before and after the tap. If the screen cannot be captured, the command reports an unknown outcome; inspect the screen before you retry.

back --system sends system back input: the Android back keyevent, the iOS back gesture, or the tvOS Siri Remote Menu button. macOS has no system back, so it reports unavailable.

orientation portrait|portrait-upside-down|landscape-left|landscape-right works on iOS and Android mobile targets only. On ADB-backed Android it turns auto-rotate off, and the lock persists after the session ends until something turns it back on. A foldable iPhone simulator (iPhone Duo) refuses portrait-upside-down, and refuses every rotation in a scoped simulator set (--ios-simulator-device-set).

orientation auto hands rotation back to the sensor on ADB-backed Android, local or Limrun (accelerometer_rotation=1, user_rotation untouched), and reports orientation: "auto". It does not wait for the display to rotate, because there is no target rotation: the sensor decides, and an emulator usually settles on portrait. Every other backend refuses auto with UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION.

action-button presses the iPhone or iPad Action Button once. It takes no arguments, no hold duration, and no --settle, and it doesn't activate the session app or drive Camera Control. Other platforms refuse it, and a model without the button (an iPhone SE, most iPad simulators) fails with UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION.

action-button reports that the press was dispatched, not what it triggered. Simulators run no Shortcuts or App Intents, so verify the outcome on a physical iPhone. Expect a press to take about five seconds on a Simulator.

hardware-button <button> presses one phone hardware key once, with no hold and no --settle, and it doesn't activate the session app. The names are volume-up, volume-down, power, mute, sleep, wake, media-play-pause, media-next, media-previous, media-rewind, and media-fast-forward. The response reports the dispatched press, not what the OS did with it: which audio stream a volume press moves, which media session a media key reaches, and whether the HUD shows is device behavior the command does not claim.

Android presses all eleven keys on phones and tablets: the ADB-backed and helper paths send input keyevent, and an Appium-backed device presses the same keycodes through its mobile: pressKey route. A physical iPhone or iPad presses volume only, through the local runner or Appium's volume button press; no Apple leaf presses the other keys. iOS Simulators refuse volume (XCUIDevice exposes no volume press there), and Android TV and tvOS targets refuse with a pointer to tv-remote.

A power press toggles the Android screen. sleep turns it off and wake turns it on without toggling, so wake the screen with hardware-button wake after a press that turned it off. After a press that turns the screen off, later commands may hit a locked screen.

Fold a foldable device:

fold closed|half-open|open sets the pose of a foldable iPhone simulator (iPhone Duo) or a foldable Android emulator (pixel_9_pro_fold, pixel_10_pro_fold, 7.6in Foldable) and reports the pose only after confirming it on the device. Re-snapshot after every fold, even an interrupted one; refs and coordinates from before it are stale. On iOS, expect 2–4 seconds once the helper is built; half-open waits for two agreeing hinge reads one second apart. The first fold on a host or Xcode also compiles the helper and takes longer.

The iOS response names the lit panel and its size, marked coordinateSpace: "native-panel". That size is not the next snapshot's viewport and cannot place a tap.

iOS only: --keyframes plays a timed trajectory instead of a preset, for example fold --keyframes '[{"atMs":0,"angle":0},{"atMs":1667,"angle":160},{"atMs":3333,"angle":100},{"atMs":5000,"angle":180}]'. Use 2–64 keyframes starting at 0ms, strictly increasing integer timestamps up to 60,000ms, and angles from 0 to 180°.

iOS needs an Xcode with the iOS simulator SDK and foldable HID support (verified on Xcode 27.1); Device Hub and Accessibility permission aren't required. The first fold builds a helper cached under ~/.agent-device/fold-helper, which also reads the hinge back. Build and dispatch failures report fold-helper-build-failed or fold-hid-dispatch-failed; readback outcomes are listed below.

COMMAND_FAILED with reason: fold-pose-unverified means the hinge reports another pose; fold-pose-unsettled means it reached half-open but never came to rest; fold-pose-dispatched-unverified means the pose was sent but the first hinge-angle read returned no sample, so check the lit panel with a screenshot; hingeReadFailure holds the read's own failure.

UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION covers single-panel devices (single-panel-device on Android). Physical devices are refused. An iOS simulator in a scoped --ios-simulator-device-set folds the same way as one in the default set.

On Android, fold confirms the pose from the device state the emulator commits and reports hingeAngleDegrees as the hinge sensor reads it: the angle the AVD profile defines for the posture, such as 0°, 90°, and 180° on the Pixel folds or 15°, 90°, and 165° on the generic 7.6in Foldable. It also dismisses the lock screen that folding to the cover display can raise. For panels, poses, and timings, see agent-device help foldable.

Simulate an incoming call or SMS:

telephony call <number> starts an incoming call from <number> on an Android emulator; telephony accept <number> answers it and telephony cancel <number> ends it. telephony sms <number> <text> delivers a text message from <number>. Use it to check how an app reacts when a call or message arrives, for example whether video playback pauses and resumes.

The events go through the emulator console (adb emu gsm call|accept|cancel, adb emu sms send), so they work on Android emulators reached through the local adb executor. Other adb executors, such as an ADB provider, have not been verified. Physical Android devices refuse with UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION and reason: unsupported-device-kind; iOS, macOS, tvOS, web, Linux, HarmonyOS, Vega, and Limrun and WebDriver (Appium) sessions refuse with UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION too: agent-device sends telephony only through adb and does not drive Appium's own call or SMS simulation.

<number> is digits with an optional leading +, up to 15 digits. Quote the SMS text, or pass it as the remaining words; the text is sent as one argument, with backslashes and line breaks (LF, or CRLF sent as LF) escaped for the emulator console. Tabs, lone carriage returns, and other C0 or C1 control characters are refused.

The emulator console answers some events with an error, such as accept for a number with no call. That fails with COMMAND_FAILED, reason: telephony-console-refused, and the console's own consoleReason. cancel for a number with no call succeeds, because the console answers it with OK.

The emulator drops SMS characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, such as emoji, and delivers the rest of the text. textLength counts the text as sent.

The call screen or message notification can cover the app. Re-snapshot before using refs from before the event.

Remote daemons and tenants:

--tenant, --session-isolation tenant, --run-id, and --lease-id enforce lease admission on tenant-scoped daemons.

--daemon-base-url http(s)://host:port[/base-path] calls a remote HTTP daemon directly instead of starting a local one. Add --daemon-auth-token <token> (or AGENT_DEVICE_DAEMON_AUTH_TOKEN) for non-loopback daemon URLs.

Screenshots and recordings from a remote daemon are downloaded to the path you pass, so screenshot page.png and record start session.mp4 work as they do locally. record start without a path downloads to recording-<timestamp>.mp4 (.webm on web) in your working directory.

To drive a Mac's simulators and devices from another machine, see Remote Proxy. For hosted devices in CI, see BrowserStack, AWS Device Farm, or TestMu AI. For connect --remote-config, see Remote Metro workflow.

agent-device open "https://example.com" --platform ios           # open link in web browser
agent-device open MyApp "myapp://screen/to" --platform ios       # open deep link to MyApp
agent-device back --platform ios                                 # tap visible app back UI only
agent-device back --system --platform ios                        # use edge-swipe or remote back action
agent-device reinstall MyApp /path/to/app-debug.apk --platform android --serial emulator-5554
agent-device open com.example.myapp --platform android --serial emulator-5554 --session my-session --relaunch
agent-device metro reload

Human Takeover

Use takeover with an active remote connection when a person needs to use its leased device
without racing the agent:

agent-device takeover --session remote-session
agent-device takeover status --session remote-session
agent-device takeover release <hold-id> --session remote-session

takeover holds the device until you press Ctrl+C. While it holds, state-changing commands fail with
DEVICE_IN_USE and details.reason: "human_control_active"; read-only diagnostics still work. It
needs a device-scoped remote lease, so local sessions aren't supported. Holds don't survive a daemon
restart; reconnect and take the hold again. See Remote Proxy.

Web Automation

--platform web drives a browser through agent-browser and requires Node 24+. Use it when a browser step belongs inside an agent-device session, replay, batch, MCP, or Node.js client flow. For standalone browser automation, use agent-browser directly.

Set up and verify the managed web backend before you open a web session:

agent-device web setup
agent-device web doctor
agent-device open "https://example.com" --platform web
agent-device snapshot -i --platform web
agent-device get text @e2 --platform web
agent-device is visible 'label="Welcome"' --platform web
agent-device find text "Welcome" exists --platform web
agent-device click @e12 --platform web
agent-device hover @e14 --settle --platform web
agent-device fill @e13 "test@example.com" --platform web
agent-device wait text "Welcome" --platform web
agent-device network dump 25 --include headers --platform web
agent-device audio probe start 10 1000 --platform web
agent-device audio probe status --platform web
agent-device audio probe stop --platform web
agent-device screenshot ./artifacts/web-home.png --platform web
agent-device screenshot ./artifacts/web-full.png --platform web --fullscreen
agent-device viewport 1280 900 --platform web
agent-device close --platform web

web setup installs a pinned agent-browser backend into the agent-device state directory (--state-dir, AGENT_DEVICE_STATE_DIR) and reuses it when present. Run it before first use and in CI bootstrap: web commands never install the backend themselves and use only that managed install. web doctor verifies it.

Supported: URL open, snapshot refs, get text/attrs, is visible/hidden/exists/absent/focused/text, find text/selector, click/press, hover, fill/type, wait, network dump, audio probe, screenshot, close, and replay scripts made from those commands.

hover <@ref|selector|x y> moves the pointer without pressing so hover-gated UI (row toolbars, menus) appears. Add --settle to read what it revealed; on web, --settle needs a selector or coordinate target because web refs carry no geometry.

audio probe start [durationSeconds] [bucketMs] samples HTML media elements into RMS/peak dBFS buckets; see Debugging & Profiling.

Not supported: tab/window/devtools control, network routing/interception/HAR, cookies/storage, downloads/uploads, arbitrary page scripting, multi-page orchestration, and raw browser diagnostics. Use agent-browser directly for those.

Device isolation scopes

agent-device devices --platform ios --ios-simulator-device-set /tmp/tenant-a/simulators
agent-device devices --platform android --android-device-allowlist emulator-5554,device-1234

--ios-simulator-device-set <path> limits simulator discovery and commands to that simulator set. iOS physical devices are not listed while it is set.

If the selected Xcode can't resolve a scoped simulator for the Apple runner, the runner start fails with details.reason: "simulator_set_destination_not_found", naming the set and, when known, the Xcode version.

--android-device-allowlist <serials> limits Android discovery and selection to comma- or space-separated serials.

Set the same scopes with the iosSimulatorDeviceSet and androidDeviceAllowlist config keys, or AGENT_DEVICE_ANDROID_DEVICE_ALLOWLIST. CLI flags override environment values, except under a strip session lock, which ignores conflicting per-call selectors.

Start the daemon with AGENT_DEVICE_IOS_SIMULATOR_DEVICE_SET=<path> to scope every iOS simulator request to one simulator set. A request without --ios-simulator-device-set uses that set, so iOS physical devices are not listed on that daemon. A request naming a different path string, including the same path with a trailing slash, fails with INVALID_ARGS and details.reason: "ios_simulator_device_set_outside_daemon_set". macOS and other non-iOS requests ignore the set, and the host Mac stays listed. A daemon that the CLI starts inherits the CLI's environment, so later CLI calls with a different value still use the first value until the daemon restarts.

Scope applies before --device, --udid, and --serial, so an out-of-scope selector fails with DEVICE_NOT_FOUND.

On macOS, daemon startup removes any symlink at ~/Library/Developer/XCTestDevices, including one you made yourself (for example to move it to another volume), and restores XCTestDevices.agent-device-backup when it exists. A symlinked XCTestDevices is not supported. Only the link is removed, never the directory it points to; daemon.log records each step and any failed restore, which doesn't stop the daemon.

Device discovery

agent-device devices
agent-device devices --platform ios
agent-device devices --platform android
agent-device devices --platform harmonyos
agent-device devices --platform vega --target tv
agent-device devices --platform ios --ios-simulator-device-set /tmp/tenant-a/simulators
agent-device devices --platform android --android-device-allowlist emulator-5554,device-1234
agent-device capabilities --platform android
agent-device capabilities --session checkout --json

devices lists available targets after applying --platform and isolation scopes.

Each device carries model (such as iPhone 17 Pro or Pixel 9) and osVersion (such as 26.1 or 16) when platform tooling reports them: simctl for iOS simulators, devicectl or xctrace for physical iOS devices, and ro.product.model and ro.build.version.release for running Android devices. Android emulators report the system image model, such as sdk_gphone64_arm64. Stopped AVDs and other platforms omit both fields. They describe a device and are not selectors.

capabilities lists the commands the session device, or an explicit --platform/--device/--udid/--serial target, supports. JSON output includes device and availableCommands; use availableCommands instead of keeping your own platform support table. Android also reports targetReadiness.press: "bounded-geometry" when element presses check moving targets before dispatch. Test harnesses can use that capability to delegate tap readiness instead of adding a fixed transition delay. It does not wait for the result of the tap.

HarmonyOS command boundary

HarmonyOS support uses HDC and ArkUI uitest. On API 24 devices it supports lifecycle and HAP deployment, ArkUI snapshot/screenshot and selector reads, one-pointer touch and text actions, keyboard enter/dismiss, app logs, foreground app state, process RSS samples, and settings clear-app-state. Run agent-device capabilities --platform harmonyos for the command list of a selected device.

gesture pan|fling|swipe and swipe use single-pointer input. Multi-touch gestures and target-authored gesture drag return UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION.

Physical devices support whole-screen recording with record start <path> --scope device or --scope system, without --fps, --quality, or --hide-touches. Emulator recording is rejected.

Not available: orientation, clipboard, alerts, network/audio capture, push and app-event delivery, React Native helpers, and trace capture. settings supports only clear-app-state. perf memory sample reports process RSS; frame health and memory snapshots are unavailable.

Diagnostics

agent-device doctor
agent-device doctor --platform ios
agent-device doctor --platform android --app com.example.myapp
agent-device doctor --remote --json

doctor diagnoses device, app, Metro, and React Native setup for the selected target. It is read-only: it never boots, installs, or changes the device.

--platform ios|android|vega|macos|linux|web|apple limits checks to one backend; without it, doctor checks every discoverable target.

--app <id-or-name> adds app checks (install state, Metro and React Native wiring) for one bundle id or app name.

--remote runs only the checks that don't need a booted device; use it in CI bootstrap.

Prepare Apple runner

agent-device prepare ios-runner --platform ios --timeout 240000

In Apple CI setup, run prepare ios-runner after the device is booted and the app is installed, before the first snapshot, replay, or test. It builds or reuses the Apple runner, starts it, and checks that it answers.

--timeout <ms> is one budget shared by the Simulator boot and runner preparation; see Navigation.

In JSON output, buildMs, connectMs, and healthCheckMs may overlap (connectMs includes buildMs when the runner is built). Use timing.additiveParts for additive phase totals.

A cached runner that fails its health check is rebuilt once, and a runner stuck at launch is relaunched once.

CI may cache ~/.agent-device/apple-runner/derived when the cache key includes the exact agent-device package contents and Xcode version. A cached runner whose files no longer match their recorded digests is rebuilt.

Each runner source or Xcode change creates a new key under ~/.agent-device/apple-runner/derived/<platform-folder>/. After a build, agent-device deletes, on a best-effort basis, keys that are neither among the 3 last used nor used in the last day, and never one a build is holding or a live runner lease names; change the count with AGENT_DEVICE_IOS_RUNNER_CACHE_KEEP (see Configuration). A key that can't be deleted is reported as a runner_xctestrun_cache_eviction_failed warning. A custom AGENT_DEVICE_IOS_RUNNER_DERIVED_PATH is never swept or trimmed.

runner_cache_uncertifiable means the build products couldn't be verified, for example a product outside the derived-data root, an unreadable entry, a file over 128 MB, or a socket. Point AGENT_DEVICE_IOS_RUNNER_DERIVED_PATH at a plain directory you own, or replace the tree as the error hint describes.

~/.agent-device/ios-runner belongs to older agent-device versions and is never touched. Delete it with rm -rf ~/.agent-device/ios-runner once no such version runs.

Runner build and start output goes to the session's runner.log; daemon.log covers daemon startup.

tv-remote is TV-only. Android phones, iPhones, and WebDriver (Appium) sessions refuse it with UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION.

All three TV backends support up, down, left, right, select, menu, home, and back. power and sleep can turn the screen off. A successful response confirms that the button was sent; it does not verify playback, volume, or display state, and it does not wait for the app to settle.

Android TV: app listing reads LEANBACK_LAUNCHER and LAUNCHER activities together; app launch prefers LEANBACK_LAUNCHER and falls back to LAUNCHER when the app declares no leanback activity. tv-remote sends ADB keyevents; longpress <button> selects the long-press preset, and any positive --duration-ms uses Android's longpress keyevent, which has no exact hold time.

On the device, enable ADB debugging in Settings > My Fire TV > Developer options, then adb connect <device-ip>:5555 and use --platform android --target tv. Discovery reads the amazon.hardware.fire_tv system feature, so a Fire TV that declares no leanback feature is still detected as a TV target and runs the Android TV backend. The Android snapshot helper requires Android 6.0 (API 23) or newer.

Helpers that are simulator-only on iOS, such as settings and push, are simulator-only on tvOS too. tvOS refuses multi-touch gestures such as gesture pinch.

Commands go through the SDK-matched Vega CLI and VDA. The VVD supports app open/close, back, home, and the eight navigation buttons listed above, with exact holds.

Some Fire TV devices ship with Vega OS instead of Fire OS. Desktop targets

agent-device devices --platform macos
agent-device open TextEdit --platform macos
agent-device open --platform macos --surface desktop
agent-device snapshot -i --platform apple --target desktop

--platform macos, or --platform apple --target desktop, selects the host Mac as a desktop target.

agent-device automates Electron and other Chromium-based macOS apps through the macOS accessibility tree. On the native backend, snapshot turns the app's Chromium accessibility tree on before reading it; once on, the tree stays on for the app's lifetime, so other surfaces see it too. See the Chromium note under the native backend below.

Use an app session for normal app control: open, snapshot, click, fill, press, scroll, back, screenshot, record. In app sessions, screenshot captures the app window, not the whole desktop.

Use the other surfaces to inspect desktop-wide UI before choosing an app, mainly with snapshot, get, is, and wait: frontmost-app is the focused app, desktop is the visible windows across the desktop, and menubar is the active app's menu bar and system menu extras. To click or fill inside one app afterwards, open it in an app session.

open <app> --platform macos attaches to a copy of the app that is already running, including one you started yourself from a script or supervisor. It opens that copy by its own app path, so another build registered for the same bundle ID, such as an earlier dev build at another path, does not start beside it. If that copy has not finished registering with macOS, the open waits briefly for it before handing the URL over, so a copy that registers within that window keeps the arguments it was started with; a copy still unregistered after the wait, or copies running from more than one path, get the plain open -b, which can start a second instance.

open <app> --platform macos --surface menubar targets one app's menu bar extras. Prefer it for status-item apps, which often expose little through the app surface.

Prefer selectors and @refs; window positions shift between runs, so raw x/y is less stable. Use click --button secondary for context menus, then run snapshot -i again.

On frontmost-app and menubar, press and click post synthetic mouse events (desktop is inspect-only). --hold-ms keeps the button down (at least 40 ms, default 60 ms), --count sends independent clicks, and --double-tap sends double-click pairs. Apps like Finder read two clicks at the default interval as one double-click; pass an --interval-ms longer than the system double-click time to keep them apart. Long schedules get the time they need, and a cancelled or interrupted click releases the button. --jitter-px is ignored on these surfaces.

macOS also supports clipboard read|write, trigger-app-event, logs, network dump, audio probe, alert, and part of settings (see Settings helpers). audio probe samples host system audio and needs Screen Recording permission; see Debugging & Profiling.

Mobile-only commands are unsupported on macOS: boot, shutdown, home, orientation, app-switcher, action-button, fold, install, reinstall, uninstall, install-from-source, and push.

XCTest opens bring the named app to the front. open --surface frontmost-app takes no app target and opens the app that is already frontmost. --foreground requests an initial snapshot; it does not choose activation. Run agent-device help macos for the versioned contract.

Set AGENT_DEVICE_MACOS_APP_BACKEND=native to run macOS app sessions without XCTest. There is no Automation Mode overlay, the app can stay behind other windows, and your pointer stays yours while a drawn pointer shows each action.

With the native backend, each app you open on the app surface is a device of its own. Several agents can drive different apps of one Mac at the same time, in one daemon or in daemons that share a claims directory. Two sessions on the same app conflict. A desktop, menubar, or frontmost-app session holds the whole Mac, so it conflicts with every app session. open --wait waits for a conflicting session in the same daemon only; another daemon's session refuses the open at once. An app session:

Opens its app in the background, so the frontmost app stays in front.

Opens and closes only its own app. open <url> opens the link in that app. Use a new --session for another app or surface.

Refuses clipboard, settings, and audio probe, which act on the whole Mac, with UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION (reason: unsupported-device-scope). Use a --surface desktop session for them.

Cannot see UI that another process shows, such as a system permission prompt.

Copies of one app need distinct bundle ids. Screenshots run one at a time across the Mac. Use one agent-device version per claims directory.

click, press, and fill use accessibility actions on the element at the target point, which must be inside one of the app's on-screen windows, not its menu bar. type inserts at the focused control or falls back to key events. scroll moves the scroll bar under the front window's center. Electron and other Chromium-based desktop apps expose their web content in the snapshot: the first snapshot turns the app's Chromium accessibility tree on, and a snapshot warns when that tree did not populate. screenshot captures only the app's front window, even when it is covered. The front window is the app's frontmost visible, nonempty normal-level (layer-0) window on the current Space: floating palettes and app-modal alerts at window level 8 are skipped, and a sheet is captured as its own window. If that window cannot be captured, screenshot fails; it never captures another window.

record, prepare, back, longpress, --hold-ms, --double-tap, --button secondary, gestures, and clicks on an element with no accessibility action fail with UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION (reason: unsupported-device-backend). Use the default XCTest backend for those.
